issues.legal_issue: A reversioner may maintain a declaratory suit challenging a Hindu female limited owner's pre-existing alienation despite the subsequent commencement of the Hindu Succession Act.
material_facts: A widow had alienated her husband's estate before the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
A daughter sued representatively for the reversioners, seeking a declaration that the alienation was not binding on them.
The Act came into force while the alienees' appeal was pending, and the High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that reversionary rights no longer existed.
issues.conclusion: The suit remained maintainable. The High Court's contrary decree was set aside, and the appeal was allowed for the High Court to hear the remaining merits.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14, 15 and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 do not abolish reversionary rights in property already alienated by a Hindu female before the Act came into force. A reversioner may sue for a declaration that such an alienation was made without legal necessity and is not binding on the reversioners. The Court followed Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Sera Veerayya and Brahmadeo Singh v. Deomani Missir.

predicates.representative_reversioner_declaratory_s: A reversioner brought a declaratory suit in a representative capacity on behalf of the reversioners.
predicates.pre_act_limited_owner_alienation: A Hindu female limited owner alienated property before the relevant succession-law change came into force.
predicates.alienation_challenged_as_without_legal_n: The suit challenged the alienation as made without legal necessity and as not binding on the reversioners.

issues.definition: When a representative reversioner brings a declaratory suit challenging a limited owner's pre-existing alienation as without legal necessity, the suit remains maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal is not a nullity merely because a person who died before its filing is named as a respondent, if the appeal can proceed against the surviving respondents.
material_facts: The widow died before the petition of appeal was filed in the Supreme Court.
The deceased widow was nevertheless named as a respondent in that petition.
The alienees who were surviving respondents remained parties to the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The deceased person could not be a respondent, but the appeal could proceed against the other respondents on the footing that the deceased person was not a party.
issues.legal_principle: A person who has died before an appeal is filed cannot be shown as a party respondent. That defect does not prevent the appeal from proceeding against the surviving respondents where it can be adjudicated against them. The Court also noted that the appeal against the deceased respondent had abated after no substitution order was obtained under Order XVI, rule 12(a) of the Supreme Court Rules.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal seeking relief against other parties to the dispute.
predicates.person_died_before_appeal_filing: A person named as a respondent had died before the appeal was filed.
predicates.surviving_respondents_remain: Other respondents against whom the appeal can proceed remained parties.

issues.definition: If a respondent died before an appeal was filed and other respondents remain, the appeal proceeds without the deceased person.

issues.legal_issue: The heirs of a widow who dies during a reversioner's declaratory proceeding are not necessary parties when no relief is sought against the widow personally and effective relief can be obtained against the alienee.
material_facts: The original plaintiff sued representatively for the reversioners and sought relief against the alienees concerning the widow's alienation.
The widow had been joined, but no relief was claimed against her personally.
The widow died while the dispute was pending, and not all of her heirs were parties to the appeal.
The appellant sought the same relief against the alienees that the original plaintiff had sought, and granting that relief would not conflict with a decree in favour of the widow.
issues.conclusion: The heirs of the widow were not necessary parties, and the appeal could proceed in their absence.
issues.legal_principle: Where a widow dies during a declaratory suit challenging her alienation, the representative plaintiff represents the estate of the last full owner on behalf of the reversioners and can obtain effective relief against the alienee without the widow's heirs. The Court relied on Bijoy Gopal Mukherji v. Krishna Mahishi Debi for the related principle that reversioners suing for possession after the widow's death need not join the widow's heirs.

rule.if: reversioner_declaratory_proceeding and widow_dies_during_proceeding and no_personal_relief_against_widow and effective_relief_available_against_alienee

predicates.reversioner_declaratory_proceeding: A reversioner pursued a declaratory proceeding representatively on behalf of the reversioners.
predicates.widow_dies_during_proceeding: The widow whose alienation was challenged died while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.no_personal_relief_against_widow: The claimant sought no personal relief against the widow.
predicates.effective_relief_available_against_alien: The claimant could obtain effective relief against the alienee without the widow's heirs.

issues.definition: When a widow dies during a representative reversioner's declaratory proceeding, her heirs are unnecessary if no personal relief was sought against her and effective relief remains available against the alienee.

issues.legal_issue: A declaratory suit that was proper when instituted does not become defective because reversioners become entitled to possession during its pendency, but possession cannot be decreed without amendment of the claim.
material_facts: At the institution of the suit, the reversioners were not entitled to possession and the next reversioner sought a bare declaration.
The reversioners became entitled to possession after the widow died while the proceeding was pending.
The plaint was not amended to include a claim for possession.
issues.conclusion: The later entitlement to possession did not defeat the declaratory suit. Without amendment, a decree for possession could not be granted; the reversioners would need to bring a suit for possession within the limitation period to obtain that relief.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 did not bar a bare declaratory suit where the claimant was not entitled to possession when the suit was instituted. A suit that was properly brought for a declaration does not become defective merely because further relief becomes available during its pendency. But possession cannot be decreed without amendment of the plaint, and a separate possession suit must be brought within limitation if the plaint is not amended.

rule.if: declaratory_suit_proper_at_institution and no_possession_entitlement_at_institution and possession_entitlement_arises_during_suit and no_possession_amendment

predicates.declaratory_suit_proper_at_institution: The claimant brought a declaratory suit that was proper when it was filed.
predicates.no_possession_entitlement_at_institution: The claimant was not entitled to possession when the suit was instituted.
predicates.possession_entitlement_arises_during_sui: The claimant became entitled to possession while the suit was pending.
predicates.no_possession_amendment: The claimant did not amend the pleading to seek possession.

issues.definition: A properly instituted declaratory suit survives a later entitlement to possession, but possession requires an amended claim or a separate timely suit.

issues.legal_issue: Persons who were not parties to the lower-court appeal cannot be added as respondents to a further appeal without permission, and their names may be struck from the record.
material_facts: Several relatives were added as respondents to the petition of appeal in the Supreme Court.
Those persons had not been parties to the appeal in the High Court.
No order permitting their joinder in the Supreme Court appeal had been obtained, and the appellant did not object to striking their names.
issues.conclusion: The names of those respondents were struck from the record.
issues.legal_principle: A person who was not a party to the appeal below cannot be joined as a respondent in the further appeal without an order permitting joinder.

predicates.further_appeal: A party filed a further appeal from a lower-court appellate decision.
predicates.person_not_party_to_lower_appeal: A person named as a respondent in the further appeal had not been a party to the appeal in the lower court.
predicates.no_permission_for_joinder: No court order permitting that person's joinder in the further appeal had been obtained.

issues.definition: In a further appeal, a person who was not a party to the lower-court appeal and was joined without permission is removed from the record.
